These ten questions cover the whole of Chapter 2, from what a model is to how a pipeline keeps an evaluation honest. Answer each one before opening the feedback; the explanation under every option says why it is right or wrong, so a wrong guess is as useful as a right one. Aim for eight or more before starting [Lab 2](labs/lab-02-first-ml-project.html).

::: {.checkpoint title="Supervised or not?"}
You have 5,000 compounds, each with a measured IC₅₀ against a kinase, and you want a model that predicts IC₅₀ for new compounds. Which kind of problem is this?

- [x] Supervised learning (regression)

  Correct: every training compound comes with a numeric label (its IC₅₀), and the goal is to predict that label for new inputs. A numeric target makes it regression rather than classification.
- [ ] Unsupervised learning

  Unsupervised methods such as clustering or PCA work on inputs *without* labels. Here you have a measured label for every compound and want to predict it, which is the definition of supervised learning.
- [ ] Supervised learning (classification)

  It would be classification if the target were a category such as "active / inactive". IC₅₀ is a continuous number, so this is regression. (You could turn it into classification by thresholding, but that throws information away.)
:::

::: {.checkpoint title="What does the loss do?"}
In linear regression, what role does the mean squared error loss play during fitting?

- [x] It measures how far the current predictions are from the labels; fitting means choosing the parameters that make it as small as possible

  Correct: the loss turns "how wrong is the model?" into a single number of the parameters, and fitting (by the normal equation or by gradient descent) is the search for the parameters that minimise it on the training data.
- [ ] It is reported as the final test metric and nothing else

  The loss is the quantity *optimised* during training. You may also report it (or its square root, RMSE) on the test set, but its defining role is to guide the fit.
- [ ] It counts how many predictions are exactly right

  Exact matches are essentially never achieved with a continuous target. MSE averages the *squared distance* between predictions and labels, so every prediction contributes, not just the exact hits.
:::

::: {.checkpoint title="A baseline that worries you"}
A colleague reports 90% accuracy for a classifier that flags toxic compounds. The dataset contains 9 non-toxic compounds for every toxic one. What is the first thing to check?

- [x] The accuracy of a `DummyClassifier` that always predicts "non-toxic", which would also be 90%

  Correct: with 90% of compounds non-toxic, predicting "non-toxic" for everything scores 90% while finding no toxic compound at all. A model that does not beat that baseline has learned nothing. Every reported score needs a baseline next to it.
- [ ] Whether they used `random_state=42`

  A fixed seed makes the result reproducible, but reproducibly meaningless is still meaningless. The seed does not tell you whether 90% is good.
- [ ] Whether the model used enough features

  More features might help or hurt, but the question is whether 90% is impressive at all. Compare against the trivial model before worrying about the real one.
:::

::: {.checkpoint title="MAE or RMSE?"}
Two solubility models have the same MAE of 0.8 logS, but model A has RMSE 0.9 and model B has RMSE 1.5. What does the difference tell you?

- [x] Model B makes a few very large errors; model A's errors are more uniform in size

  Correct: RMSE squares the errors before averaging, so a handful of large misses inflate it far more than they inflate MAE. Equal MAE with a larger RMSE means a heavier tail of big errors. The gap between the two numbers is itself diagnostic.
- [ ] Model B is better because a larger RMSE means more variance explained

  RMSE is an *error*: smaller is better. Variance explained is R², a different quantity, and it falls as RMSE rises.
- [ ] Nothing: MAE and RMSE always move together

  They often do, but not here. RMSE can never be smaller than MAE, and how much larger it is depends on how unevenly the errors are distributed.
:::

::: {.checkpoint title="A negative R²"}
A regression model has R² = −0.3 on the test set. What does that mean?

- [x] The model's predictions are worse than always predicting the mean of the target

  Correct: R² compares the model's squared error with that of the constant mean prediction. R² = 0 means "as good as the mean"; a negative value means the model does worse, which happens with a badly overfitted or badly mis-specified model evaluated on new data.
- [ ] A bug: R² is a squared quantity, so it cannot be negative

  Despite the name, R² is defined as 1 minus a ratio of squared errors, and that ratio can exceed 1 on held-out data. On the *training* data of an ordinary least-squares fit it cannot be negative; on the test set it can.
- [ ] The model explains 30% of the variance, with the sign indicating a negative correlation

  R² is not a correlation and carries no direction. 0.3 would mean 30% of the variance explained; −0.3 means the model is worse than the mean baseline.
:::

::: {.checkpoint title="Spotting overfitting"}
You fit a model and evaluate it both on its training data and on a held-out test set. Which pattern is the clearest sign that it is overfitting?

- [x] Training error is tiny and the test (or cross-validated) error is much larger

  Correct: a large gap between training and held-out performance is the signature of a model that has memorised the training examples, including their noise. This is also why the training score is never evidence on its own: fitting chose the parameters to make exactly those errors small. Simplify the model, regularise it, or get more data.
- [ ] Training error and test error are both high

  Both high means the model has not captured the signal at all: that is *underfitting*. A straight line through curved data behaves like this. The cure is a more flexible model or better features.
- [ ] The test error is slightly lower than the training error

  A small difference either way is normal sampling noise, and a test error slightly *below* the training error is not a problem. If it were far below, you would suspect leakage, not overfitting.
:::

::: {.checkpoint title="Ridge versus lasso"}
You have 200 descriptors and suspect only a dozen matter. You want a model whose coefficients tell you which ones. Which penalty should you reach for, and why?

- [x] Lasso (L1), because it drives many coefficients exactly to zero and so performs feature selection

  Correct: the L1 penalty on the sum of absolute coefficients has corners that make exact zeros the optimum for weak features. The surviving non-zero coefficients are your selected descriptors. Scale the features first, or the penalty is unfair across units.
- [ ] Ridge (L2), because it sets unimportant coefficients to zero

  Ridge *shrinks* all coefficients towards zero but almost never makes any of them exactly zero. It is excellent for stabilising a model with correlated features, but it will not hand you a short list.
- [ ] Neither: a penalty only makes the fit worse on the training data

  A penalty does raise training error slightly, by design: it trades a little bias for a lot less variance, and usually *lowers* the test error. That trade is the point of regularisation.
:::

::: {.checkpoint title="Why cross-validate?"}
Compared with a single train/test split, what does 5-fold cross-validation give you?

- [x] A less noisy estimate of generalisation error, using every sample once as a test sample, and a sound way to choose hyperparameters without touching the test set

  Correct: each fold is a different train/validation split, so the average score is less dependent on which molecules happened to land in the held-out set. It also gives a spread across folds. Hyperparameter choices made this way leave the final test set untouched for the one evaluation at the end.
- [ ] A model trained on five times as much data

  Each fold trains on 80% of the training data, not on more data than you have. The benefit is a better *estimate*, not a bigger model.
- [ ] Permission to skip the test set, since cross-validation already measures generalisation

  Cross-validation scores are used to *choose* between models and settings, which makes them slightly optimistic for the winner. A separate, untouched test set is still needed for the final number.
:::

::: {.checkpoint title="Precision or recall in a screen?"}
You screen a 100,000-compound library with a classifier and will test the predicted actives experimentally; the assay is expensive, so you can afford only 500 compounds. Which metric matters most for the compounds you send to the assay?

- [x] Precision: of the 500 you test, you want as many true actives as possible

  Correct: precision is the fraction of predicted positives that are really positive. With a fixed, small assay budget, every false positive costs a slot, so you raise the decision threshold to keep precision high and accept that some actives are missed.
- [ ] Recall: you must find every active compound in the library

  Recall is the fraction of all true actives that the model flags. Maximising it means flagging many compounds, which you cannot afford to test. Recall matters when missing a positive is the costly error, for example in a diagnostic test.
- [ ] Accuracy: the overall fraction of correct predictions

  With actives rare, accuracy is dominated by the correctly predicted inactives and barely changes with how well you find actives. It is the wrong summary for an imbalanced screen.
:::

::: {.checkpoint title="Leaks and pipelines"}
Which of these workflows gives a test score that overstates how the model will do on new data?

- [x] Fitting a `StandardScaler` and selecting the 20 features most correlated with the target on the full dataset, then splitting and evaluating

  Correct: both steps are fitted before the split, so they have seen the test rows. The scaler leak is small, but selecting features by their correlation with the *target* on all rows bakes the test labels into the feature set. On pure noise this produces a positive test R². Fit every preprocessing step inside a pipeline, on training data only.
- [ ] Fitting a pipeline of `StandardScaler` and `Ridge` on the training set and calling `.score` on the test set

  This is the correct workflow: the pipeline is one estimator, so `fit` learns the scaler from the training rows only and `.score` merely applies it to the test rows. Inside `GridSearchCV` the same guarantee holds fold by fold.
- [ ] Removing exact duplicate molecules before splitting

  Removing duplicates *before* the split is the fix, not the leak. Duplicates that straddle the split would let the model be tested on molecules it has memorised.
:::
